metric: CPU time of the core (src/gcm.c and its envelope) relative to bare OpenSSL EVP AES-256-GCM, which draws a random nonce as the core's random seal does
gate: for each size, the seal and open ratios (the core over bare EVP) and the det ratio (the core's deterministic seal over a bare deterministic seal of the same shape) must be at most the matching ceiling; the core's deterministic seal over its random one is recorded, never gated
runner_cpu: to be recorded from the bench workflow
note: A ratio, never nanoseconds, so it is portable across runners. Each benchmark runs five times in a random order and the gate reads the median of the raw repetitions. The ceilings are per size because the core's fixed per-call cost is a larger share of a small message; sizes live in tests/bench/benchmark.cc (kSizes). Both sides of det pay the same two HMAC-SHA256 passes over the plaintext and the same AES-GCM, so det is like-for-like whatever the runner's CPU accelerates. The deterministic seal over the random one is not like-for-like — it compares a SHA-256-bound seal with an AES-bound one — and an O17 probe found it ranging from about 1.3 to 9.6 across sizes and GitHub runners, whose AES-GCM throughput differed about 5x while SHA-256 barely moved, so it is recorded, not gated. Refresh recorded_ratios and tighten a ceiling toward the observed worst only when it holds across runs and both libcryptos.
